Q: How do streams and asyncEngine count work together in CUDA A:

Is this just a flag or is there any impact?

It's a flag, a capability indicator. I think basically all CUDA GPUs are capable of running concurrent kernels. I'd be very surprised if anyone came across a CUDA GPU that doesn't have that capability.

I think concurrent kernels only make sense if streams are used, right?

Yes, to arrange any sort of concurrency in CUDA (two or more things happening at the same time) its usually necessary to make proper use of streams. There are a few minor exceptions to this, such as the concurrency of host code execution and device code execution.

Is this the number of kernels that can possibly run in parallel as given above.

No it is not. An async engine in CUDA can be thought of as a DMA engine, and it is needed/used any time you issue an asynchronous data transfer request (e.g. cudaMemcpyAsync) that has the actual capability to run asynchronously. In order to make the transfer happen asynchronously, a hardware engine is used, and that engine is called an async engine. Async engines have no usage or bearing with respect to kernel activity, except that using an async engine would allow, for example, a data transfer activity to happen at the same time as a kernel is executing, subject to various requirements and device capacity.

This leads me to a more general question about streams. How many streams can be used or allocated at all? For example if the asyncEngineCount is 3, does it even make sense to have more than 3 streams?

There isn't a specified upper limit to the number of streams that can be created. I have seen properly designed codes that use 40+ streams. Streams have no direct connection to the asyncEngineCount. If you create and use more streams than the amount of device connections, the streams will distribute themselves ("alias") across device connections, but device connections also has nothing explicit to do with async engines.

What would happen if I allocate more streams than asyncEngineCount and let multiple kernels run concurrently? Lets assume I allocate 10 streams and run 10 kernels concurrently, but the asyncEngineCount only has 3. Would CUDA only run 3 kernels at a time and the other ones are blocked until a stream is free?

Nothing unusual would happen. There is no connection between asyncEngineCount and streams, or the number of kernels you can execute concurrently. Concurrent kernel execution depends on factors and resources that have no connection to asyncEngineCount, and you can certainly demonstrate more than asyncEngineCount kernels running concurrently, and the last time I checked, the concurrentKernels sample code does that. There is an upper bound/hardware limit (see table 18) to the number of concurrent kernels, but it has no relation to async engines.

I couldn't find a good explanation around async execution and streams,

For general CUDA learning, I usually recommend this online training series and the section on "CUDA Concurrency" has relevant information for this topic. The programming guide also has an extended section on Asynchronous Concurrent Execution in CUDA.

Q: How do people handle naming for path strings versus path objects? A:

In modern Python, in code under my control, I convert to a pathlib.Path as soon as I can and always pass that around. This addresses the naming ambiguity you describe, gives you a richer API, and makes it immediately clear in type annotations what the value is.

def replace_string_in_file(file: Path, original: str, replacement: str) -> None:
  ...

If it's unavoidable, or if it will clarify things, you can have the variable name end in "path". For example, in a FastAPI route (where variable names become HTTP query parameters) you might say

UPLOAD_DIR: Path = ...

@app.get("/something")
def something(path: Annotated[str, Query()]) -> None:
  if "/" in path:
    raise ValueError("invalid path")
  upload_path = UPLOAD_DIR / path
  ...

I don't personally like an ambiguous str | Path parameter, in part because I often enough want to write code that can operate on a file content. So, is the "string" form "foo.csv", or "col1,col2\n1,2,3\n"? You'll also inevitably wind up immediately normalizing it to either a string or a Path immediately so you don't have duplicated code paths, and it'd be better to name the specific type you need up front.

Q: How can I filter out specific column from a CSV file in Perl? A:

You can use some of Perl's built in runtime options to do this on the command line:

$ echo "1,2,3,4,5" | perl -a -F, -n -e 'print join(q{,}, $F[0], $F[3]).qq{\n}' 1,4

The above will -a(utosplit) using the -F(ield) of a comma. It will then join the fields you are interested in and print them back out (with a line separator). This assumes simple data without nested comma's. I was doing this with an unprintable field separator (\x1d) so this wasn't an issue for me.

See http://perldoc.perl.org/perlrun.html#Command-Switches for more details.
